optionReasons.saa-med-225:option:1: Timeout major does not change the search pattern — each invocation continues to call the Secrets Manager; only increases the function.
optionReasons.saa-med-225:option:2: Environment variable with manual update breaks automatic rotation — old credentials until someone remembers to update.
optionReasons.saa-med-225:option:3: It's the closest because hiding out of the handler is real pattern and would solve latency — but the global variable lives until the container dies: a rotation in the middle leaves the Lambda with old password and failed connection; caching library/extension has TTL that recapturing the rotated secret.

finalJustifications: Because caching library/extension hides the secret in memory with TTL: latency and cost fall, and periodic searching captures rotations without intervention.
Because Extension receives from Secrets Manager a push at each rotation, injecting the new password into the function without any retracement.
Because the caching library shares the secret between all the executions of the account, and a single search supplies the entire fleet.
Because Extension moves authentication out of the handler, and runtime itself signs connections to the database.

optionReasons.saa-med-226:option:1: SCPs have no 'created by group X user' condition — apply to whole accounts/OUs, and roles do not 'herit group restrictions''.
optionReasons.saa-med-226:option:2: Tag in creation does not limit the permissions of the created roll — 'company policy' without technical strength is not ceiling.
optionReasons.saa-med-226:option:3: It's the closest because a Deny from SCP in fact would block access — but the SCP reaches OU/account INTEIRA, not 'the roles created by developers': in the same environment it would also knock down legitimate applications; the selective ceiling by delegated roll is the Boundary Permissions required in iam:CreateRole.

finalJustifications: Because Boundary Permissions is the roof of IAM for delegation: the condition in iam:CreateRole forces every role created to load the boundary that denies the production pocket.
Because the bandary intercepts the calls to the prod-data and redirects them to the test pocket, protecting the data without breaking the code.
Because the boundary is inherited automatically by all the roles of the account as soon as the administrator creates it, without additional condition.
Because the boundary replaces the policies of the roles of the developers, who become only the permissions listed in it..

optionReasons.saa-med-227:option:1: Safe protects storage, but access key remains static and long-lasting — exactly what you want to remove.
optionReasons.saa-med-227:option:2: It's the closest because it involves STS and TakeReal Roll — But TakeReal Needs a Credentials to Be CHAMADO: private network does not authenticate anyone, and 'reliance by IP of origin' does not replace identity; X certificate exchange.509 by credentials STS is the IAM Roles Anywhere.
optionReasons.saa-med-227:option:3: Anonymous identity of Cognito is for public apps with minimal access — inadequate for corporate workloads to publish in SQS.

finalJustifications: Because the Roles Anywhere changes the X certificate.509 of CA reliable by credentials STS temporary — the on-premises application publishes in the SQS no static key accesses.
'Cause Roles Anywhere installs an agent STS location in the data center, which issues credentials without contact with the cloud of AWS.
Because Roles Anywhere converts the legacy application into an instance EC2 logical, eligible for Forum Profile and native role.
Because the Roles Anywhere fed the Active Directory directly into IAM, and each publication in SQS use the Kerberos ticket from the host.

optionReasons.saa-med-228:option:1: It's the closest because cost is actually a real criterion between the two — but it's INVERTIDO: o Parameter Store Standard is free and the Secrets Manager collects by secret/month and by calls; no one migrates to him by economy, but by managed rotation.
optionReasons.saa-med-228:option:2: There is no relevant difference in latency — and 'multipurpose = slow' is invented reasoning, not characteristic of service.
optionReasons.saa-med-228:option:3: False: The SecureString of Parameter Store supports CMK of the customer normally — encryption KMS doesn't differentiate between the two.

finalJustifications: Because the managed rotation is the differential: the Secrets Manager change the password in RDS And update the secret via Lambda managed, without manual intervention.
Because Secrets Manager synchronizes the new password with the Parameter Store of the other accounts, propagating each rotation by the organization.
Because Secrets Manager authentic a Lambda direct at the bank by IAM, eliminating the password itself and the need to rotate it.
Because Secrets Manager version the complete bank password history, allowing to restore old credentials in rollback.

optionReasons.saa-med-229:option:1: It's the closest because the tool is SQL injection — but the SQLi match rule inspects SQL in the content, not the NOME of the User-Agent tool: 'sqlmap' in the header is not syntax SQL; blocking a specific string in a header is the string match rule.
optionReasons.saa-med-229:option:2: Rate-based rule does not filter by User-Agent in the thread like that — and 1 request/5min would block any IP visitor.
optionReasons.saa-med-229:option:3: Core Rule Set protects against generic patterns — does not guarantee blocking by User-Agent 'sqlmap' specifically, which is the request.

finalJustifications: Because the string match rules with 'Contains' in the header User-Agent home any request containing 'sqlmap' and applies Block — exactly the filter requested.
Because the string match rule consults the list of malicious tools of AWS and blocks the known signatures of sqlmap.
Because the string rule returns a CAPTCHA to sqlmap, and the automated tool fails the challenge and abandons the attack.
Because the string match rule rewrites the suspicious User-Agent before ALB, neutralising the injection without discarding the request.

optionReasons.saa-med-230:option:0: S3 is accessed via API public/endpoints — permission does not depend on VPN or Direct Connect between accounts.
optionReasons.saa-med-230:option:1: The opposite: roles access resources from one's own account normally — it's the most common case of all.
optionReasons.saa-med-230:option:2: It is the closest because it moves on the right concept (type of credentials) — but reverses reality: the S3 accepts temporary roll credentials normally; assumed roles are the recommended access pattern, and the scenario lock comes from the bucket policy, not the type of credentials.

finalJustifications: Because in cross-account access the destination pocket needs to explicitly authorize the roll in the bucket policy — the IAM policy alone is not enough as in the intra-account.
Because the empty Bucket Policy activates the Block Public Access by default, which treats the assumed role as public access and rejects it..
Because without a bucket policy, S3 requires ACLs per object, and the bucket objects do not have ACL granting reading to the external role.
Because the bucket policy is the only place where S3 validates the ExternalId of the role, mandatory in any access between accounts.

optionReasons.saa-med-232:option:0: Multiple consumers in the same row is the normal drawing of SQS — every message goes to a consumer at a time via visibility timeout.
optionReasons.saa-med-232:option:1: Failure to order does not create duplicate — out-of-order requests remain separate requests for business.
optionReasons.saa-med-232:option:2: It's the closest because visibility timeout short CAUSA real redeliveries — but it's just an aggravating factor: even with perfect timeout, the Standard line is at-last-once by design and can duplicate; the root cause is the delivery semantics, and the robust solution is FIFO or idempotence.

finalJustifications: Because Standard is at-last-once by design — duplicates are expected; FIFO (exactly-once per group) or the consumer's equal power resolves at root.
Because the Standard line only duplicates messages above 256 KB, and dividing requests into smaller messages eliminates problem.
Because at-last-once mode is a row configuration, and just switch the attribute to exactly-once in the Standard row itself.
Because the duplicate delivery comes from the long polling of consumers, and the short polling ensures a single reading per message.

optionReasons.saa-med-234:option:1: It's the closest because it correctly describes the behavior FIFO by group — but changing the row type does not ISOLA the poisonous message: it would continue to hold its own group forever; taking the message off the path after N failures is Dead Letter Queue with maxReceiveCount.
optionReasons.saa-med-234:option:2: Visibility timeout of 24h only hides the problematic message for longer — it returns and locks the queue again.
optionReasons.saa-med-234:option:3: SSE rest cryptograph — no 'integrity validation that discards corrupted message' in the description.

finalJustifications: Because the DLQ with maxReceivecount=3 moves the poison message to quarantine after the third failure — the main row continues to flow and the case is investigated separately.
Because the DLQ repair corrupted messages using the metadata of SQS and return them to the main row already ready to process.
Because the DLQ prioritizes valid messages in delivery, lowering those that failed to end the queue every new attempt.
Because the DLQ notify the producer to forward the original image, replacing the corrupted message with its full version.
